newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaitis, worried about security, vote in poll.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaitis, worried about security, vote in poll.

text.p: Kuwaiti men on Monday voted in the second parliamentary election since the 1991 Gulf War ended Iraq's occupation of the oil-rich state.
"Security and the economy are looming very high" in this election, said parliament's political adviser Abdullah al-Shayeji.

He said last month's tension between Washington and Baghdad and the October 1994 Iraqi buildup on the border showed Kuwaitis how vulnerable their small country was, pushing "genuine security concerns to the front burner".

Analysts forecast that more than 70 percent of the 107,000- strong all-male electorate would vote. Polls opened at 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) for 12 hours. About 230 candidates, including 41 members of the outgoing parliament, are standing.
Women are not allowed to run or vote.
Some of the 50 new MPs are expected to press for further defence measures to deter Iraq, while also seeking stronger powers to monitor state spending and tackle alleged corruption.

The outgoing parliament, the only elected house in the six Gulf Arab states, was no rubber stamp. It opened probes into alleged official corruption and claims of poor government management before Iraq's 1990 invasion and occupation of Kuwait.
Speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun said in his closing address on Saturday that parliament "defended public funds and held accountable those who allowed themselves to violate its sanctuary."
He had earlier criticised the state for not moving fast enough to rebuild the military five years after the war which ended Iraq's seven-month occupation.

Incidents since the Gulf War have shown that Kuwait and most of its sparsely populated Gulf Arab allies, among the world's largest arms importers, will continue to depend on the United States and other Western powers.
About 90 minutes after polls opened some 10 percent of the electorate in some districts had already casted their votes. There are some 200 polling stations and results are expected early on Tuesday.
Moslem Shi'ite candidate and former deputy Abdel-Mohsen Jamal told Reuters after he cast his vote that he was happy with the election process so far.

Interior Minister Sheikh Ali Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah told the state's television as he visited polling stations "What is clear is that organisation and security is very good, maybe even almost excellent."

A Western diplomat said despite repeated allegations of vote-buying by pro-government and other candidates none of the leading politicians was questioning the fairness of the process or calling for international monitoring.
Jamal said although there might be "a change of faces in the new parliament I do not expect a major change in the political affiliations" of the new MPs.
Shayeji said late on Sunday "Islamists will hold their own".
The last parliament, elected in 1992, had 16 Moslem Sunni and Shi'ite Islamists. It was made up of 50 elected MPs and 11 ministers who by law become ex-officio deputies.
